# Predicates

## Two Weeks Ago {.smaller}

You filled this in, in week 2. Two of these rows are propositions. Five are not.

::: {.fillable}
| # | Statement | Proposition? |
|:-:|---|:--:|
| 1 | If it's a kitten, then it's a cat. | |
| 2 | If an animal is a mammal, then it is a cat. | |
| 3 | If I'm an only child, then I have zero siblings. | |
| 4 | If I eat breakfast, then I ace the quiz. | |
| 5 | A player is in the NHL only if they are a professional. | |
| 6 | To be empty, a string must have length 0. | |
| 7 | No song appears on the Hot 100 without reaching #1. | |
: {tbl-colwidths="[6,72,22]"}
:::

::: notes
3 and 4 only. Both are about a fixed "I" -- one particular person -- so each is
true or false and that is the end of it.

The other five are not about anything in particular. "If it's a kitten, then
it's a cat" -- which animal? There is no answer, because the sentence does not
name one. It is not true and it is not false. It is waiting.

I deliberately did not say this in week 2. Today it gets a name.
:::

## Predicates {.smaller}

\

$p$: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ ate cereal for breakfast.

\

We may want to apply the statement to many students, so we define a **predicate**.

\

-   $P(x)$: $x$ ate cereal for breakfast.

-   $x$ can be *instantiated* to a particular student, or an arbitrary one.

-   $P(\underline{\hspace{2em}})$ is a proposition.

::: notes
The blank is the whole idea. A predicate is a proposition with a hole in it,
and nothing is true or false until the hole is filled.

Go back to row 1 with this: P(x) = x is a kitten, C(x) = x is a cat. Now the
sentence has a shape -- but it still is not a proposition, because x is still
loose. That is the next section.
:::

## Which Cheerios? {.smaller}

In week 3 we said: for Cheerios, $\neg(p \vee q)$.

$p$: a cereal has less than 4 units of protein &emsp;&emsp; $q$: a cereal has more than 6 units of sugars

::: {.fillable}
| Cereal | protein | sugars | $p$ | $q$ | $\neg(p \vee q)$ |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Cheerios | 6 | 1 | | | |
| Apple Cinnamon Cheerios | 2 | 10 | | | |
| Honey Nut Cheerios | 3 | 10 | | | |
| Multi-Grain Cheerios | 2 | 6 | | | |
: {tbl-colwidths="[40,12,12,12,12,12]"}
:::

::: notes
F F T  /  T T F  /  T T F  /  T F F

So the claim was true of exactly one of them. "Cheerios" was never the subject
-- a ROW was. p and q were predicates all along, and each row instantiates
them.

Ask which row we meant in week 3. The honest answer is that the question was
not well formed until today.

Real numbers from data/cereal.csv, 77 cereals.
:::

## Every Row at Once {.smaller}

A dataframe is a domain. Each row instantiates the predicate, and gets a truth
value of its own.

\

Of the 77 cereals:

::: {.fillable}
| | Cereals |
|---|:-:|
| $p$ — protein $< 4$ | \_\_\_\_ |
| $q$ — sugars $> 6$ | \_\_\_\_ |
| $\neg p \wedge \neg q$ | \_\_\_\_ |
: {tbl-colwidths="[70,30]"}
:::

::: notes
66, 39, 9. Counted from the file.

The nine survivors: 100% Bran, All-Bran, All-Bran with Extra Fiber, Cheerios,
Life, Maypo, Quaker Oat Squares, Quaker Oatmeal, Special K.

A filter is a predicate evaluated once per row, keeping the rows where it comes
out true. That is all a Boolean mask is, and they have been writing them since
DSCI 100 without the name.
:::

## Boolean Masks

Select all the cereals with at least 4 units of protein and no more than 6 units of sugars.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_cereal
import pandas as pd
cereals = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-CS/dsci220/refs/heads/main/data/cereal.csv')
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_cereal
p = cereals['protein'] < 4
q = cereals['sugars'] > 6
filtered_df = cereals[______]
filtered_df
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_cereal
#| check: true
correct_answer = cereals[(cereals['protein'] >= 4) & (cereals['sugars'] <= 6)]
ok = (
    len(filtered_df) == len(correct_answer)
    and filtered_df.index.equals(correct_answer.index)
)
feedback = (
    {"correct": True,  "message": "Nine cereals survive. That is a predicate, evaluated 77 times."}
    if ok else
    {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. You want neither p nor q: ~p & ~q."}
)
feedback
```

::: notes
Answer: cereals[~p & ~q], or equivalently ~(p | q) -- De Morgan, and worth
running both to show they agree.

By filtering, they are defining a predicate instantiated by each row and
evaluating its truth value. Say that sentence.
:::

# Quantifiers

## Quantified Predicates {.smaller}

Consider the predicate

|        $H(x)$: $x$ is a hero

Is this a proposition? \_\_\_\_\_\_

\

We add a **quantifier** to bind the variable:

\

|   $\forall$ &emsp; "for every", "for all"
|   $\exists$ &emsp; "there exists", "there is at least one"

\

|        $\forall x\, H(x)$ &emsp;&emsp; $\exists x\, H(x)$

\

Now? \_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
No, then yes. The variable is free in the first and bound in the second, and
binding is what closes the hole.

Worth saying: a quantifier needs a domain. "Everyone is a hero" -- everyone in
what? For the cereal frame the domain was the 77 rows, which is why we could
just count.
:::

## Counterexample {.smaller}

Someone says "all comedians are funny," and you disagree.

\

|        $\forall x,\ C(x) \rightarrow F(x)$

\

Your immediate response: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

\

This evidence of refutation is called a \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

::: notes
"No -- what about THIS one?" You name a comedian who is not funny.

Counterexample. And note what it takes: ONE. To refute a "for all" you need a
single case, which is why the negation of a universal is an existential:

  ~forall x P(x)  ==  exists x ~P(x)

They met this shape in week 2 without knowing it -- refuting "if you eat
breakfast you ace the quiz" took exactly one morning where you did and did not.
:::

## Witness {.smaller}

Someone says "there is a funny comedian," and you disagree.

\

|        $\exists x,\ C(x) \wedge F(x)$

\

Their immediate response: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

\

This evidence of justification is called a \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

\

Aside: why not $\exists x,\ C(x) \rightarrow F(x)$?

::: notes
They name one. A witness.

So the asymmetry: one case SETTLES an existential and one case DESTROYS a
universal. Neither can be settled the other way round without checking the
whole domain -- unless the domain is small enough to exhaust, which is exactly
the distinction from lecture 1.

The aside: C(x) -> F(x) is true whenever C(x) is FALSE, so "there exists x with
C(x) -> F(x)" is satisfied by any non-comedian. It claims almost nothing. With
"exists" you want AND; with "for all" you want ->. That pairing catches
everyone once.
:::

## Words and Ideas

Predicate, instantiation

Free and bound variables

Domain

$\forall$, $\exists$

Counterexample, witness
